rationale: Read the retained receipt of experiment 7bf97b230d24477d93e10e441f0cd5c1-experiment (CheckRun e1ee764584564a95b3e288381dfb75d9, exit 0, 19 events). Both declared comparisons for the authority-transition question are violated at index 18, so that question is recorded as a witnessed violation with its behavior entry. The same clean run also reproduced the stale-configuration chain (events 11 and 12), the repair path (15, 16) and the pinned configuration index (14), so the acknowledged-write account gains a second, independent run of the same harness file as reproducibility evidence via joint_history.

knowledge.statement: A server that is no longer part of the configuration can still make a voter campaign and displace the serving leader by sending a TimeoutNow request: the handler stores the transfer trigger without inspecting the sender, and the resulting campaign carries the leadership-transfer flag that suppresses voters' rejection for nodes that already know a leader.
knowledge.conditions: A configuration from which the sending server has been removed while it remains transport-reachable; the request is sent over the transport to a surviving voter; the receiving voters know a healthy leader.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the transfer trigger is not restricted to the current leader, so a non-member can displace a healthy leader. Parsed event 17 records the state before the request: the removed node is not in the configuration in force and the target is a follower. Parsed event 18 records the outcome after the removed node's TimeoutNow arrived: the target became leader, leadership_changed is true, old_leader_stepped_down is true, and the request returned no error. Both declared comparisons are violated at index 18, in a run whose exit code is 0. Mechanism from source: timeoutNow clears the known leader, sets the recipient's state to Candidate and stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer without looking at the request's RPCHeader, so any transport-reachable peer can trigger the exchange; the election that follows sets LeadershipTransfer on its vote requests, and requestVote skips its leader-availability rejection when that flag is set, so voters that already know a healthy leader still grant. The candidate-membership rule is still applied, which is why the trigger is effective through a legitimate member: the removed node supplies only the trigger, and the receiving voter campaigns.
counterevidence: The consequence is disruption of authority rather than loss of committed data: logs, terms and entries stay consistent and the cluster elects again after the term bump.

Any cluster member can already force term changes by campaigning; what makes this path distinct is that it bypasses the voters' leader-availability protection, which normally rejects campaigns while a leader is known.
The probe delivered the request from the removed node's own transport in an in-memory cluster, which is the situation of a server taken out of the configuration but not shut down.
limitations: Measured on one three-voter in-memory cluster with the repository's own test facilities; elections are timing-dependent, so which node leads afterwards is not the decisive observation, only that leadership changed.
The removed node's request carried its own RPC header, which the handler ignores; no authentication or authorization layer outside the transport was modelled.
The account covers the transfer trigger and the vote path; it does not measure how often such churn could recur or how long the cluster stays without a leader.

interpretations.joint_history: Two separate runs of the same harness file produced the same chain, one as the experiment's own receipt (1766eefaf1f14339ad1cff36e02a7c33) and one inside the later clean run whose exit code is 0 (e1ee764584564a95b3e288381dfb75d9, events 9, 11 and 12). Both runs started the node under test with the snapshot's three-voter configuration while the configuration in force had five voters, acknowledged a write held by only two of five voters, and ended with a leader elected from the configuration in force that did not hold the payload.
interpretations.rationale: Current account, now supported by two runs: the configuration gap makes an acknowledged write unsafe. In the first receipt, event 9 shows the restarted node with the snapshot's three-voter configuration while the configuration in force has five voters and the log still holds a configuration entry beyond the snapshot; event 10 shows it leading with that set; event 11 shows an Apply returning nil while only two nodes held the payload, below the three acknowledgements the configuration in force requires; event 12 shows a leader elected from the five-voter configuration whose log store has no entry carrying the payload. The second run reproduces the same three decisive observations at its own indices 9, 11 and 12, and its exit code is 0. Mechanism from source: the restart applies logs up to the recovered commit index and the scan then starts after it, so the recommitted configuration entry never reaches processConfigurationLogEntry; the leader's quorum and commitment set come from the recovered configuration, so commitment.recalculate advances the commit index on the (n-1)/2-th match index of the smaller voter set. The reading is payload-based: the later leader reports the same last-applied index the acknowledged entry had, but a different entry occupies it.
counterevidence: The state needs RestoreCommittedLogs with a commit-tracking store, a snapshot taken while a smaller configuration was committed, and later entries advancing the recovered commit index past the recommitting entry; a cluster that snapshots after every configuration change may not reach it.

Any later configuration entry or an installed snapshot repairs the recovered configuration, which the same clean run shows for the empty-configuration case, so the window closes once the node receives one; the harness prevents that repair for the node under test.

Both holders of the acknowledged entry were stopped for the final reading, so the observation establishes absence from the new leader rather than permanent erasure if a stopped holder rejoins; the entry was nevertheless one that a true majority had not stored.
limitations: Measured on in-memory five-voter clusters with the repository's in-memory transport, commit-tracking store and mock FSM; production stores, real network timing and concurrent client traffic are not covered.
The harness orchestrates a leadership transfer, a transport disconnection and the shutdown of the two holders, so the ordering is the harness's, though every step uses public APIs.

The reproduced run comes from the same harness file with one tolerance added for the case where the restarted node had already won an election, so the second run exercises the same phases but not an independent construction.
